t.textos.enuma-elish.version: Standard Babylonian version, 7 tablets (about 1,100 lines), probably composed toward the end of the 2nd millennium BC; Neo-Assyrian copies from Nineveh and Assur and Neo-Babylonian and late copies from Babylon, Uruk, Kish and Sippar
t.textos.enuma-elish.estructura.0.sinops: Before heaven and earth had names, Apsu (fresh water) and Tiamat (salt water, the sea) mingle their waters, and from them generations of gods are born: Lahmu and Lahamu, Anshar and Kishar, Anu and Ea (Nudimmud). The uproar of the young gods disturbs Apsu, who with his vizier Mummu plans to destroy them. Ea puts him to sleep with a spell, kills him and founds his dwelling on top of him; there Marduk is born. Tiamat, urged on by other gods, creates eleven monsters and raises Qingu (Kingu) as her husband and chief, handing him the Tablet of Destinies.
t.textos.enuma-elish.estructura.1.sinops: Ea learns of Tiamat's preparations and reports them to Anshar. Ea and then Anu are sent against her, but they return without daring to face her. Anshar then proposes Marduk, who agrees to fight on condition that the assembly grant him the supreme power to decree the destinies.
t.textos.enuma-elish.estructura.2.sinops: Anshar sends his vizier Kakka to Lahmu and Lahamu to summon the gods; the messenger repeats in full the account of Tiamat's preparations (long formulaic repetitions). The gods gather at a banquet, drink and, in high spirits, accept Marduk's condition.
t.textos.enuma-elish.estructura.3.sinops: The gods enthrone Marduk and test his power by making a constellation disappear and reappear with his word. Marduk arms himself with bow, mace, net and the seven winds, mounts his storm chariot and defeats Tiamat; he captures her allies and snatches the Tablet of Destinies from Qingu. He splits Tiamat's body in two: with one half he makes the sky and sets up the Esharra as the dwelling of Anu, Enlil and Ea.
t.textos.enuma-elish.estructura.4.sinops: Marduk organizes the sky: stations of the great gods in the stars, the year and the twelve months, the station of Nēberu (his own star), the course of the Moon and the Sun. From Tiamat's body he makes the Tigris and the Euphrates flow from her eyes and forms mountains. The gods pay him homage and he announces the founding of Babylon.
t.textos.enuma-elish.estructura.5.sinops: Marduk decides to create the human being (lullû) to bear the labor of the gods. Ea carries out the plan with the blood of Qingu, declared guilty of the rebellion. Marduk divides the gods into Anunnaki of heaven and of the Underworld; these, grateful, build Babylon and the Esagila temple. A banquet and the first listing of Marduk's names.
t.textos.enuma-elish.estructura.6.sinops: The proclamation of Marduk's fifty names continues and concludes, each with its theological and etymological explanation. The epilogue orders that the poem be preserved, taught by the learned and recited, and that fathers pass it on to their sons.
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.0.texto:
When on high the heaven had not been named,
and the earth beneath did not yet bear a name,
and the primeval Apsu, who begot them,
and chaos, Tiamat, the mother of them both,
mingled their waters together,
and no field was formed, no marsh was to be seen;
when none of the gods had been called into being,
and none bore a name, and the destinies [were not fixed];
then the gods were created in the midst of [heaven],
Lahmu and Lahamu were called into being […].
The ages grew […];
then Anshar and Kishar were created, and over them […].
Long were the days; then there arose […]
Anu, their son, […]
[…]
Nudimmud, whom his fathers, [his] begetters […],
abounding in all wisdom […],
was exceedingly strong […],
he had no rival […].
Thus were established and [… the great gods (?)].
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.0.fuente: Spanish version based on L. W. King, The Seven Tablets of Creation (1902), vol. I, pp. 3–5 (public-domain translation; lines 15–16, very fragmentary, have been omitted), translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.0.nota_acad: The ancient title of the poem is its first two words, enūma eliš, "when on high". Apsu is the fresh underground water and Tiamat (from tâmtu, "sea") the salt water; the word "chaos" is a gloss by King: the Akkadian says mummu Tiāmat, where mummu is an epithet of disputed meaning ("creator", "mother"). King was working with very broken copies from Nineveh; today the text is practically complete (Lambert 2013; Talon 2005). His restoration of line 9, "in the midst of [heaven]", has been superseded: the line says that the gods were created "within them", that is, in the bosom of the mingled waters. The gaps in lines 10–21 are filled with confidence today: Anu is born "in the likeness" of Anshar and begets Nudimmud (Ea). Line 6 speaks of reed huts or beds and marshes, the landscape of southern Mesopotamia: the world before creation is imagined as a formless delta.
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.0.lectura_a: In The 12th Planet (1976), Sitchin reads the first lines as a planetary cosmogony: Apsu would be the Sun, Mummu Mercury and Tiamat a watery planet between Mars and Jupiter; the divine pairs would be the planets that gradually formed, and the theogony the birth of the solar system.

The text does not identify any of these gods with planets: Apsu and Tiamat are personified bodies of water (fresh and salt), and line 5 says so explicitly ("they mingled their waters"). The astral identifications of the Mesopotamian gods (Venus with Ishtar, Jupiter with Marduk, etc.) are well documented in astronomical texts such as MUL.APIN, and they do not match Sitchin's. The Babylonians knew only five planets visible to the naked eye; there is no trace in the texts of Uranus, Neptune or a "planet" Tiamat.

Catherine Keller reads Marduk's confrontation with Tiamat as the ancient model of a "tehomophobia" (from tehom, the deep of Genesis 1:2): the fear of the watery, feminine, undifferentiated depths that Western culture has sought to dominate. She proposes recovering the primordial as a womb and not as an enemy.
Catherine Keller, Face of the Deep: A Theology of Becoming, 2003
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.1.texto:
[They raged, they plotted evil without rest] night and [day].
[They prepared for battle], fuming and raging;
[they joined their forces] and made war.
[Ummu-Hubu]r, who formed all things,
[made besides] invincible weapons; she spawned monster serpents,
[sharp of] tooth, merciless of fang;
[with venom instead of] blood she filled [their] bodies.
Fierce [monster vipers] she clothed with terror,
[with splendor] she decked them, [she made them] of lofty stature.
[Whoever] beheld them, terror overcame him;
their bodies reared up and none could withstand [their attack].
[She set up] vipers, and dragons, and the (monster) [Lahamu],
[and hurricanes], and raging dogs, and scorpion-men,
and mighty [tempests], and fish-men, and [rams];
[they bore] cruel weapons, without fear [of battle].
Her commands [were mighty], [none] could resist them;
in this way, huge of stature, [she made] eleven (monsters).
Among the gods, her sons, because he had [given her support],
she exalted Kingu; in their midst [she raised him] to power.
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.1.fuente: Spanish version based on L. W. King, The Seven Tablets of Creation (1902), vol. I, pp. 17–19, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.1.nota_acad: Ummu-Hubur ("Mother Hubur", the name of the river of the Underworld) is here an epithet of Tiamat. This passage is repeated word for word three more times in Tablets II and III, a typical feature of Akkadian epic. King filled in many words in brackets, and several of his identifications of the eleven monsters have been superseded: the list is read today as mušmaḫḫu (supreme serpent), ušumgallu (great dragon), bašmu (horned serpent), mušḫuššu (serpent-dragon, Marduk's animal on the Ishtar Gate), laḫmu ("the hairy one", not the goddess Lahamu), ugallu (great lion-demon), uridimmu (raging dog or lion-man), girtablullû (scorpion-man), ūmū dabrūtu (fierce storms), kulullû (fish-man) and kusarikku (bull-man, not "ram"). All of them later appear as defeated guardians in the iconography of temples and amulets.
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.1.lectura_a: Sitchin interprets Tiamat's eleven creatures as her eleven satellites and Kingu as the largest of them, which after the cosmic collision would have become the Earth's Moon.

The poem describes composite animals with fangs, venom and weapons, which have a long independent iconographic history (the mušḫuššu, the scorpion-man, the fish-man) on seals, reliefs and protective figurines. No Mesopotamian text identifies Kingu with the Moon, which is the god Sin/Nanna, with his own cult at Ur and Harran. The number eleven is symbolic, and in other traditions the list of defeated enemies varies.
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.2.texto:
Then Tiamat and Marduk, the counselor of the gods, advanced;
into the fight they rushed, they drew near to battle.
The lord spread out his net and caught her,
and the evil wind that (came) behind him he let loose in her face.
When Tiamat opened her mouth as wide as she could,
he drove in the evil wind before she could close her lips.
The terrible winds filled her belly,
and her courage was taken from her, and she opened her mouth wide.
He seized the spear and burst her belly,
he cut through her inward parts, he pierced (her) heart.
He overcame her and took away her life;
he cast down her body and stood upon it.
[…]
Then the lord rested, gazing upon her corpse,
while he divided the flesh of the […] and devised a cunning plan.
He split her like a flat fish into two halves;
with one half of her he made a covering for the heavens.
He fixed a bolt, he posted a watchman,
and bade them not to let her waters come forth.
He passed through the heavens, he surveyed their regions,
and opposite the Deep he set the dwelling of Nudimmud.
And the lord measured the structure of the Deep,
and he founded the Esharra, a mansion like unto it.
The mansion Esharra, which he created as heaven,
he caused Anu, Bel and Ea to inhabit in their districts.
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.2.fuente: Spanish version based on L. W. King, The Seven Tablets of Creation (1902), vol. I, pp. 71–77, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.2.nota_acad: This is the core of the so-called Chaoskampf (struggle against chaos), a motif that H. Gunkel (Schöpfung und Chaos, 1895) related to the biblical texts about the dragon and the sea. The comparison in line 137 is understood today as "like a fish set out to dry" (nūn mašṭê): a domestic image of a fish split open in two. The cosmos is born from the corpse of the vanquished: the upper half of Tiamat is the sky, with a bolt that prevents her waters from falling (compare the "waters above the firmament" of Genesis 1:7). "Bel" is Enlil. The Esharra is a cosmic level between the sky and the Apsu. Marduk's victory has been read as a political myth: the rise of the god of Babylon to the head of the pantheon, probably reinforced after the recovery of his statue by Nebuchadnezzar I (c. 1100 BC).
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.2.lectura_a: For Sitchin the "celestial battle" is a collision: Marduk would be a wandering planet (Nibiru) that, as it crossed the solar system, struck Tiamat; one half formed the Earth and the other, shattered, the asteroid belt (the "hammered bracelet" of the sky).

The text describes a fight with weapons (net, wind, spear, mace) between two characters with a mouth, belly, heart and lips, and then the construction of a heavenly vault: half of Tiamat becomes the sky, not the Earth. A planetary collision of the kind Sitchin imagines would not leave the Earth in its present orbit nor produce an asteroid belt, whose total mass is tiny (less than 5% of the Moon's). The "bracelet" comes from Sitchin's reading of another passage, not from this text.

Tikva Frymer-Kensky sees in the Enuma Elish a stage in the displacement of the goddesses in Mesopotamian religion: the great primordial mother becomes a monster and her body the raw material of a cosmic order run by a male warrior god.
Tikva Frymer-Kensky, In the Wake of the Goddesses, 1992
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.3.texto:
He (Marduk) made the stations for the great gods;
the stars, their images, as the stars of the Zodiac, he fixed.
He ordained the year and into sections he divided it;
for the twelve months he fixed three stars.
After he had […] the days of the year […] images,
he founded the station of Nibir to determine their bounds,
that none might err or go astray.
He set the station of Bel and of Ea beside him.
He opened great gates on both sides,
he made the bolt strong on the left and on the right.
In the midst thereof he fixed the zenith;
the Moon-god he caused to shine forth, the night he entrusted to him.
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.3.fuente: Spanish version based on L. W. King, The Seven Tablets of Creation (1902), vol. I, pp. 79–81, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.3.nota_acad: A key astronomical passage. "Three stars for each month" refers to the so-called Babylonian astrolabes, lists of 36 stars (three per month in the "paths" of Anu, Enlil and Ea). King says "Zodiac", but the zodiac of twelve equal signs was only formalized in Babylon around the 5th century BC; today the phrase is rather translated as "the constellations". Nēberu (King: "Nibir") means in Akkadian "passage, ford, crossing point"; in astronomy it designates a celestial position linked to Marduk, usually identified with the planet Jupiter or with a point on its path (so in MUL.APIN and in the Enuma Elish itself, VII, where Nēberu is one of Marduk's names). The "great gates" are the gates of the horizon through which the heavenly bodies rise and set.
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.3.lectura_a: Sitchin makes Nibiru (Nēberu) the "twelfth planet", home of the Anunnaki, with a highly eccentric orbit of 3,600 years that periodically brings it close to the Earth. From 1995 Nancy Lieder (ZetaTalk) popularized the idea that Nibiru would collide with or pass close to the Earth in 2003, and later the date was moved to 2012.

In this line Nēberu is a "station" fixed by Marduk within the already ordered sky, to serve as a reference for the other heavenly bodies; not a body that arrives from outside. The Babylonian astronomical texts, which recorded the positions of the visible planets for centuries, identify Nēberu with Jupiter or with a star in Marduk's region, and never attribute to it a period of 3,600 years (the sar is simply the number 3,600 in the sexagesimal system). A planet like that would be visible and would disturb the orbits of the others; the announced dates passed without anything happening.
